title: Memory and configuration in practice
subtitle: MS-DOS 4.00 and FreeBSD 15.1, measured and read from the source

slides.title: The PC memory map seen by MS-DOS 4.00
slides.caption: Conventional, upper, high, extended and expanded memory; DOS manages only the first 640 KB
slides.notes: Walk left to right. Everything MS-DOS 4.00 itself allocates lives below 640 KB: there is no HIMEM.SYS, no DOS=HIGH and no upper-memory blocks in this release (search the tree with the class). Extended memory is reached through INT 15h by drivers that hook function 88h to claim it; expanded memory is seen through the 64 KB page frame in a gap of the UMA.

slides.title: Lab 8.1: Map the first megabyte
bullets: MEM /DEBUG: every arena block and resident driver
MEMMAP.COM: BIOS data area, INT 12h, INT 15h 88h, A20 test

Puzzle: a longer program name leaves 16 bytes less memory
slides.notes: Output 8.6 shows DOSBox-X's UMA: in text mode only B8000-BFFFF is decoded, the video BIOS is 16 KB, and C400-EFFF is empty. A20 is disabled because the MS-DOS 4.00 kernel never enables it (only some drivers do, for their own use). The puzzle is the environment block: EXEC appends the program's path, so A:\MEMORYXX.EXE needs one more paragraph than A:\MEM.EXE.

slides.title: EMS bank switching
slides.caption: Four 16 KB windows onto a pool of pages; INT 67h function 44h changes what a window shows
slides.notes: On a board the windows are switched by I/O registers; EMM386 does it with four page-table entries per window. The program can see only 64 KB of the pool at a time, and pointers into a window are valid only while the right page is mapped.

slides.title: How EMM386 answers INT 67h
slides.caption: DOS runs in virtual-8086 mode; a ring-0 monitor owns the page tables
slides.notes: INT 67h in V86 mode goes through the protected-mode IDT, whose gate 67h has DPL 3. Every call is first reflected to the real-mode vector, EMM_rEntry: allocation runs there in V86 mode, while mapping functions set EMM_Flag and issue INT 67h again to run in ring 0. The monitor also traps the A20 and DMA ports: the classic problems of a virtual machine monitor, solved in a 1988 DOS device driver.

slides.title: Mapping one EMS window: four page-table entries
slides.code:
pushf                   ; preserve direction flag
        cld                     ; forward

        stosd                   ; store 1st page table entry
        add     eax,P_SIZE      ; eax <-- next address

        stosd                   ; store 2nd page table entry
        add     eax,P_SIZE      ; eax <-- next address

        stosd                   ; store 3rd page table entry
        add     eax,P_SIZE      ; eax <-- next address

        stosd                   ; store 4th page table entry
callouts: EAX holds the pool page's physical address plus control bits
One 16 KB window = four 4 KB PTEs
_MapHandlePage reloads CR3 to flush the TLB
slides.notes: map_EMM_page in EMMP.ASM. Before this, it looked up the pool page in _pft386 and the window's first PTE in _page_frame_base. Ask why the CR3 reload in _MapHandlePage can come before these stores here.

slides.title: A processor check that never fires
slides.code:
call    Inst_chk_f
        or      ax,ax                   ; q: already installed?
        jz      chk_pt                  ; n: go check processor type
        or      [msg_flag],INS_ERR_MSG  ; y: error
        jmp     IE_exit                 ; quit
;
;  verify processor type
;
chk_pt:
        call    Is386                   ;Q: is this a 386 ?
        jnz     inc_prc                 ;  N: no, set error
callouts: chk_pt is reached only with ZF = 1
Is386 returns its answer in CF and restores the other flags
jnz is never taken; and MASM encoded it as a 386-only 0F 85
slides.notes: Two independent bugs: the wrong flag, and the encoding. Under .386p MASM 5.10 emitted near Jcc (0F 8x) for these short forward jumps, so a 286 faults on the very first conditional jump of the driver's interrupt routine. Changing eight jumps makes the 286 print 'incorrect machine type' (Exercise 8.4).

slides.title: Lab 8.4: the C heap on MS-DOS
bullets: Small model: malloc stops after 59 KB with 509 KB still free in DOS
The start-up code keeps a full 64 KB DGROUP: 256 + 6,688 + 65,536 bytes
_fmalloc takes the rest from DOS with function 48h
Large model: malloc takes DOS segments and the near heap
_ffree never gives memory back to DOS
slides.notes: Built with Microsoft C 5.10 from the MS-DOS tree. The near heap is bounded by 16-bit pointers, not by DOS. LINK /CP:1 shows that the run-time grows the block with function 4Ah when it needs to.

slides.title: Maps, objects, page queues, backing store
slides.caption: Pages arrive on first touch and move between queues; the page cache is just vnode pages
slides.notes: Processes have map entries pointing to VM objects; physical pages belong to objects and sit in the active, inactive or laundry queue or are free or wired. The page daemon ages active pages, frees clean inactive ones and sends dirty anonymous pages to swap through the laundry.

slides.title: The page queues
slides.code:
#define PQ_NONE         255
#define PQ_INACTIVE     0
#define PQ_ACTIVE       1
#define PQ_LAUNDRY      2
#define PQ_UNSWAPPABLE  3
#define PQ_COUNT        4
callouts: Laundry: dirty pages waiting for swap
slides.notes: top's Mem line (Active, Inact, Laundry, Wired, Buf, Free) reads exactly these counters with sysctl, see usr.bin/top/machine.c. Free memory is low on a busy system because file pages stay cached in these queues.

slides.title: Swap reservation and vm.overcommit
callouts: Bit 2 counts most of RAM as reservable
Bit 0 makes the allocation fail when over
slides.notes: With the default vm.overcommit=0 nothing fails here: memory is overcommitted, and if programs touch more than RAM plus swap the OOM killer in vm_pageout.c kills the largest process. On a machine without swap, bit 0 alone would make nearly every allocation fail; use 5. Root is never refused (PRIV_VM_SWAP_NOQUOTA): in the course VM only an ordinary user saw malloc fail with vm.overcommit=1.

slides.title: malloc on both systems

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00 + Microsoft C 5.10
bullets: INT 21h 48h/49h/4Ah, paragraphs
Near heap inside the 64 KB DGROUP
Far heap: segments from DOS
Fails at once and exactly: NULL
Freed memory never returns to DOS

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1
bullets: jemalloc in libc over mmap (no sbrk: JEMALLOC_DSS off)
Arenas and thread caches
Pages appear at first touch
Rarely fails; the OOM killer may act later
Freed pages purged after dirty_decay_ms, at once from 8 MiB

slides.notes: jemalloc_FreeBSD.h undefines JEMALLOC_DSS, so the allocator never calls sbrk even though libc still exports it. MALLOC_CONF and /etc/malloc.conf tune it at run time; Lab 8.6 uses dirty_decay_ms and stats_print.

slides.title: Lab 8.6: watching FreeBSD memory
bullets: sysctl hw.physmem hw.realmem hw.usermem
sysctl vm.stats.vm.*, top -o res, vmstat 1, swapinfo
touchmem: VSZ grows at malloc, RSS only when pages are touched
free: madvise(MADV_FREE); RSS and VSZ stay until the page daemon or exit
truss: mmap and madvise, no break
slides.notes: Everything in this lab runs in the FreeBSD VM; Outputs 8.17-8.19 were captured in the course VM. Blocks of 8 MiB or more go to a separate jemalloc arena with decay time 0, so MALLOC_CONF decay settings change nothing for touchmem; MADV_FREE leaves the pages mapped. Contrast with Lab 8.1: on DOS MEM accounts for every byte from the arena, on FreeBSD the accounting is by page state.

slides.title: Boot-time configuration
slides.caption: One file processed in passes, versus defaults plus overrides and ordered scripts
slides.notes: SYSINIT reads CONFIG.SYS before any shell exists; COMMAND.COM /P runs AUTOEXEC.BAT. On FreeBSD the loader reads loader.conf, the kernel reads tunables, and /etc/rc runs the rc.d scripts in the order computed by rcorder, in two passes split at FILESYSTEMS.

slides.title: /etc/rc: rcorder, twice
slides.code:
# Do a first pass to get everything up to $early_late_divider so that
# we can do a second pass that includes $local_startup directories
#
unset system_rc
find_system_scripts
files=`rcorder ${skip} ${skip_firstboot} ${system_rc} 2>/dev/null`
run_rc_scripts --break ${early_late_divider} ${rc_early_flags} $files
⋮
find_system_scripts
files=`rcorder ${skip} ${skip_firstboot} ${system_rc} ${local_rc} 2>/dev/null`
run_rc_scripts ${rc_late_flags} $files
callouts: First pass: base scripts up to FILESYSTEMS
slides.notes: The early_late_divider default is FILESYSTEMS (defaults/rc.conf line 35): until local file systems are mounted, package scripts may not exist. rcorder's errors go to /dev/null, which is why a missing provider is silent at boot.

slides.title: An rc.d script (all of it after the #! line)
slides.code:
# PROVIDE: rwho
# REQUIRE: DAEMON
# BEFORE:  LOGIN
# KEYWORD: shutdown

. /etc/rc.subr

name="rwhod"
desc="System status server"
rcvar="rwhod_enable"
command="/usr/sbin/${name}"

: ${rwhod_svcj_options:="net_basic"}

load_rc_config $name
run_rc_command "$1"
callouts: rcvar: rwhod_enable, NO in the defaults
slides.notes: run_rc_command implements start, stop, status, enable and the rest; service(8) calls the script with the same environment as at boot. Lab 8.5's heartbeat script adds daemon(8), a pid file, procname and an extra command.

slides.title: When does a change take effect?
slides.caption: MS-DOS: reboot or a TSR; FreeBSD: tunable, sysctl, service, module
slides.notes: CTLFLAG_RDTUN variables are read once while the kernel starts, for the same reason that BUFFERS= needs a reboot: data structures were sized with them. CTLFLAG_RW variables change at once; services pick up rc.conf on the next start.

slides.title: Lab 8.7: run-time knobs
bullets: KEYB IT at the prompt: 5,792 bytes resident, never returned
KEYB US switches the layout inside the resident copy
MODE changes BIOS state and exits: free
sysctl -aT (855 tunables), sysctl -aW, sysctl -d vm.overcommit
kern.maxfiles changes at run time; hw.physmem cannot
slides.notes: The DOS half is captured on MS-DOS 4.00; the FreeBSD half runs in the VM. kern.maxfiles is the counterpart of FILES=: a limit on objects allocated on demand, not a preallocated table.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Every CONFIG.SYS line has a price in bytes you can compute from the source
EMM386 used 386 paging only to imitate a 64 KB window
FreeBSD counts pages by state; free memory is meant to be low
DOS refuses allocations exactly; FreeBSD promises, then may kill
Defaults + overrides + declared order make FreeBSD mistakes local
slides.notes: Close by tying memory and configuration together: on MS-DOS configuration is mostly about memory, because every table competes for the same 640 KB and is fixed at boot. On FreeBSD configuration is about behaviour, and memory is managed by policy at run time.
